rationale: B wins because it keeps the story close to the supplied facts and asks the question that can kill the whole lead: "whether the 10% sits on top of, or absorbs, the Apple/Google in-app-purchase cut." A has good instincts, but "Millions of Unpaid Gaming Community Managers Just Got a Business Model" smuggles in a number and labor history the update does not give. That is the difference between a pitchable angle and a headline wearing a borrowed suit.
gaps_in_A: "Millions of Unpaid Gaming Community Managers Just Got a Business Model" invents scale and labor status. The update gives 200M MAU, not millions of unpaid managers.
"first real monetization product plus reported IPO preparation" is unsupported. The facts say this program is new, not that it is Discord's first real monetization product.

"Undercuts App Stores and Patreon" and "in range with Patreon and Twitch" import competitor comparisons not supplied in the update. If you need Patreon/Twitch, source them as proof, don't bake them into the angle.
It misses B's killer proof question: whether the 10% stacks on top of Apple/Google mobile payment fees. Without that, the 10%-versus-30% story may collapse on the first reporter read.
gaps_in_B: "turns 200M users into a payments business" overstates the addressable revenue base. MAU is not the same as paying subscribers, paid servers, or creator revenue.

"moving from advertising and one-off tips toward owner-run recurring subscriptions" imports platform-monetization context not in the update. It can be context after sourcing, not a factual foundation.
"Substack's 10%, Patreon's tiers" is useful beat context but not grounded in the supplied facts. Keep it in the proof file unless independently verified.
